mentions.quote: In the marriage of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, a wife of one's own class is best
A Brāhmaṇa may have three other wives in the regular order of the classes.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman are born a Cāṇḍāla (चाण्डाल), a Sūta (सूत), and a Vaidehaka (वैदेहक).
Except for the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
except for the death of a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa does not receive the death penalty

entities.description: The priestly class (varṇa) whose members are subject to distinct marriage, inheritance, and punishment rules throughout this section of the Nāradasmṛti.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas are named repeatedly as a distinct class whose legal privileges and duties differ from other varṇas across marriage, caste-mixture, inheritance, and criminal-punishment rules.

mentions.quote: In the marriage of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, a wife of one's own class is best
A Kṣatriya may have two other wives
A Kṣatriya woman should wait for six years
mentions.role: subject of waiting period for absent husband

mentions.quote: An Ambaṣṭha (अम्बष्ठ), a Māgadha (मागध), and a Kṣattā (क्षत्ता) are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman.

entities.description: The warrior/ruling class (varṇa) subject to specific marriage, waiting-period, and caste-mixture regulations in this window.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas are explicitly named in rules concerning the number of permitted wives, waiting periods for absent husbands, and offspring born from inter-varṇa unions.

mentions.quote: a Vaiśya is said to have one
A Vaiśya woman who has borne children should wait for four years
The sons of a Vaiśya woman are the Dauṣṣanta (दौष्षन्त), the Yavana (यवन), and the Āyogava (आयोगव).

entities.description: The merchant/farming class (varṇa) governed by distinct marriage and caste-mixture rules in the text.
entities.justification: Vaiśyas are named in rules limiting polygamy and specifying the mixed-caste sons born from Vaiśya women, differentiating their legal position from other varṇas.

mentions.quote: A Śūdra woman may likewise have three other husbands
No time limit is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is it a transgression of Dharma

entities.description: The servile class (varṇa) whose women are subject to more permissive remarriage rules and have no prescribed waiting period for absent husbands.
entities.justification: Śūdra women are singled out as having distinct rules regarding multiple husbands and no obligatory waiting period, marking their lower legal status in the varṇa hierarchy.

mentions.quote: For the propagation of beings, this is the creation of Prajāpati.
mentions.role: divine authority cited for remarriage provisions

mentions.quote: Therefore, Prajāpati ordained their lack of independence.

entities.description: The creator deity invoked as the divine sanction behind rules governing women's remarriage and their perpetual guardianship.
entities.justification: Prajāpati is cited twice as the ultimate divine legislator for two key legal doctrines—women's remarriage in emergencies and women's permanent dependence on male guardians.

mentions.quote: From a Brāhmaṇa woman are born a Cāṇḍāla (चाण्डाल), a Sūta (सूत), and a Vaidehaka (वैदेहक).
The most sinful in the mixed castes (`saṃkara` (संकर)) is born with two classes in between in the reverse order

entities.description: The most stigmatized mixed-caste (pratiloma) group, born from a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra man, ranked as the most sinful product of hypogamous union.
entities.justification: The Cāṇḍāla is explicitly listed among the sons born from reverse-order (pratiloma) inter-varṇa unions and is identified as the most polluted of the saṃkara castes.

mentions.quote: From a Brāhmaṇa woman are born a Cāṇḍāla (चाण्डाल), a Sūta (सूत), and a Vaidehaka (वैदेहक).
The son born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Kṣatriya is remembered as a Sūta (सूत), of the next class.
A Sūta (सूत), a Māgadha (मागध), and an Āyogava (आयोगव) are likewise sons born in the reverse order

entities.description: A pratiloma (hypogamous) mixed caste born from a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya man, listed among the sons born in the reverse order of the varṇas.
entities.justification: The Sūta is named consistently as the specific offspring of a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya father in the text's caste-mixture taxonomy.

mentions.quote: An Ugra (उग्र), a Pāraśava (पारशव), and a Niṣāda (निषाद) are born in the regular order (`anulomataḥ`)

entities.description: An anuloma (hypergamous) mixed-caste group listed among the offspring of regular-order inter-varṇa unions.
entities.justification: The Niṣāda is named as one of three anuloma castes produced in the regular order, establishing its place within the text's systematic caste taxonomy.

mentions.quote: The sons of a Vaiśya woman are the Dauṣṣanta (दौष्षन्त), the Yavana (यवन), and the Āyogava (आयोगव).

entities.description: A mixed-caste group listed as one of the three sons born of a Vaiśya woman through inter-varṇa unions.
entities.justification: The Yavana appears in the systematic list of offspring born of a Vaiśya woman in the context of the text's varṇa-mixture (saṃkara) taxonomy.

mentions.quote: The mutual desire of a willing man and a willing woman is said to be the fifth form, called Gāndharva.
The Gāndharva is common to all.

entities.description: The fifth of the eight recognized marriage forms, defined by mutual desire of both parties without parental arrangement, and declared valid for all varṇas.
entities.justification: The Gāndharva form is explicitly defined and singled out as the one marriage form common to all classes, making it a distinctive legal category in the text's marriage taxonomy.

mentions.quote: The Rākṣasa marriage is said to be from forcible abduction.
The last two are condemned.

entities.description: The seventh of the eight marriage forms, characterized by forcible abduction of the bride and condemned as improper.
entities.justification: The Rākṣasa marriage is explicitly defined by abduction and grouped with the Paiśāca as condemned forms, marking it as a legally recognized but morally disapproved category.

mentions.quote: The Paiśāca, the eighth and lowest, is from having intercourse with a sleeping, intoxicated, or mentally disturbed woman.
mentions.role: definition of the lowest marriage form

entities.description: The eighth and lowest marriage form, resulting from intercourse with a woman who is sleeping, intoxicated, or mentally impaired, condemned as the most degraded form.
entities.justification: The Paiśāca is explicitly designated the eighth and lowest marriage form, marking the nadir of the text's normative marriage hierarchy.

mentions.quote: What is given before the nuptial fire, what is given in the bridal procession, the husband's gift, and what is given by the father-in-law and mother-in-law
Woman's property (`strīdhana` (स्त्रीधन)) goes to her offspring; if she is childless, it goes to her husband
A woman who has lost all her property and her woman's property (`strīdhana` (स्त्रीधन)), who has caused an abortion
mentions.role: strīdhana cited in grounds for abandonment

entities.description: The legally recognized category of property exclusively belonging to a woman, defined by its sources (gifts at marriage, husband's gift, in-laws' gifts) and governed by its own inheritance rules.
entities.justification: Strīdhana is given a specific definition, its sources are enumerated, and its distinct inheritance path (to offspring first, then husband) is legislated, establishing it as a key legal category.

mentions.quote: When the partition of the paternal estate is undertaken by the sons, that is called 'Inheritance' (`dāyabhāga` (दायभाग))

entities.description: The legal topic covering the partition of a father's estate among his sons, heading the thirteenth chapter of litigation topics in the Nāradasmṛti.
entities.justification: Dāyabhāga is defined at the opening of the section on inheritance, establishing it as a formal legal category and naming the litigation topic that organizes subsequent rules.

mentions.quote: Whatever act is done with force by those puffed up with strength and arrogance, that is called a crime of violence (`sāhasa`)
It is further known to be of three kinds: the first, the middle, and the highest

entities.description: The legal category of crimes committed by force or arrogance, subdivided into three grades each carrying distinct punishments up to death.
entities.justification: Sāhasa is explicitly defined and then taxonomized into three severity levels, structuring the entire fourteenth chapter of litigation topics.

mentions.quote: When a man is seen together with a woman who has a husband, in another's house, it is known by the wise as adultery (`saṃgrahaṇa`)
By sending a female messenger, by sending letters, and by other signs of misconduct, all is remembered as adultery (`saṃgrahaṇa`)
By sending food or drink, or clothes, garlands, and likewise perfumes, all is remembered as adultery (`saṃgrahaṇa`)

entities.description: The legal category of adultery, broadly defined to include not just physical contact but also letters, gifts, messengers, and other communicative acts implying illicit intimacy.
entities.justification: Saṃgrahaṇa is defined at the opening of the adultery section and then repeatedly expanded to cover a wide range of indirect acts, constituting a detailed legal doctrine.

mentions.quote: The king must ensure that caste intermixture (`varṇasaṃkara` (वर्णसंकर)) does not occur.
The most sinful in the mixed castes (`saṃkara` (संकर)) is born with two classes in between in the reverse order

entities.description: The concept of inter-varṇa mixing producing mixed-caste offspring, treated as a social harm requiring active royal prevention and graded by the degree of class distance in the union.
entities.justification: Varṇasaṃkara is named as a royal prevention duty and is the organizing concept behind the entire caste-mixture taxonomy presented in this window.

themes.topic: Regulation of marriage and its eight forms

mentions.quote: Eight forms of marriage are declared for the classes, for the sake of the sacrament.
Of these, the first four, beginning with the Brāhma, are declared to be righteous. The Gāndharva is common to all. The last two are condemned.

themes.justification: The text enumerates all eight marriage forms, evaluates their moral standing, and assigns them differential legal validity, making marriage-form regulation a central organizing theme of the section.

themes.topic: Hierarchy of caste purity and the prohibition of hypogamous unions

mentions.quote: Those born in the reverse order (`pratilomāḥ`), such as the Sūta (सूत), who are born from a hypogamous union, are lower and more sinful.
The king must ensure that caste intermixture (`varṇasaṃkara`) does not occur.

themes.justification: The entire caste-mixture taxonomy of this window is organized around the distinction between anuloma (hypergamous, less sinful) and pratiloma (hypogamous, more sinful) unions, framing varṇa purity as a fundamental legal and moral concern.

themes.topic: Legal subordination of women and perpetual male guardianship

mentions.quote: The father protects her in maidenhood, the husband protects her in youth, the sons protect her in widowhood; a woman does not deserve independence.
Even women born in a noble family are ruined by independence. Therefore, Prajāpati ordained their lack of independence.

themes.justification: The text repeatedly affirms that women require a male guardian at every life stage, framing female subordination as divinely ordained and legally mandatory.

themes.topic: Rules governing property and inheritance at family partition

mentions.quote: When the partition of the paternal estate is undertaken by the sons, that is called 'Inheritance' (`dāyabhāga`).
Of these, six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are not heirs but kinsmen. Each preceding one is remembered as superior.

themes.justification: Section 13 is entirely devoted to the rules governing partition of paternal estate, preferential shares, excluded categories, and the ordered list of twelve son-types, making inheritance a major substantive theme.

themes.topic: King as ultimate arbiter and enforcer of Dharmic law

mentions.quote: The king should protect the agreements of heretics, corporations, guilds, troops, and other groups, both in fortified towns and in the countryside.
When the people prosper, the king's Dharma and treasury increase. When they decline, it declines; therefore, he should strive for their prosperity.
The king must ensure that caste intermixture does not occur.

themes.justification: Across all subsections in this window—land disputes, agreements, marriage, caste, inheritance, and violence—the king is the ultimate enforcer of law, whose prosperity is tied to the people's welfare.

themes.topic: Graded monetary punishments (amercements) calibrated to offense and class

mentions.quote: The punishment for the first, depending on the act, is at least one hundred. For the middle, it is known by the wise in the same order.
For men, in a transgression with a woman of a higher class, the highest amercement is stated; in the reverse case (with a lower class), the lowest.

themes.justification: The text systematically calibrates fines by three levels (first, middle, highest amercement) and by varṇa rank of victim and offender, making graded monetary punishment a structural theme across multiple sections.

themes.topic: Seed-and-field doctrine governing ownership of offspring

mentions.quote: Women were created for the sake of offspring; the woman is the field, and men are the sowers of seed.
When seed is cast into a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, the owner of the seed has no share in it.
Without a field, there can be no crop, nor can there be one without seed. Therefore, offspring is desired by Dharma to belong to both.

themes.justification: The text explicitly deploys the seed-and-field metaphor as a legal doctrine for determining paternity and ownership of offspring, extending it across multiple analogical cases including purchased women and wandering bulls.

themes.topic: Niyoga — appointed levirate conception to prevent family extinction

mentions.quote: If the husband of a woman who has not borne children should die, she, being appointed by her elders, should go to her brother-in-law.
But when the family is on the verge of extinction, for the sake of progeny and not out of lust, a man, appointed by his elders, may approach a kinsman's wife.

themes.justification: The text devotes several consecutive rules to the levirate practice (niyoga), regulating when it is permitted, how it must be conducted, and what offenses arise from deviating from the procedure.

themes.topic: Determination of land boundaries and resolution of agricultural disputes

mentions.quote: In a dispute over a field boundary, the decision should come from the neighbors, the elders of the town and village, and those who know the marks.
They should determine the boundary by the marks that indicate it: by chaff, charcoal, potsherds, jars, sacred sites, and trees.

themes.justification: Section 11 is wholly devoted to boundary determination, fallow field rules, dam rights, and crop damage, making agricultural land law a distinct and substantive theme in this window.

themes.topic: Corporate and guild governance (puga, śreṇi) and limits of their autonomy

mentions.quote: The established rules of heretics, corporations, and others are called an 'agreement.' The violation of that agreement is called 'Breach of an Agreement.'
But what is contrary to the king's interest, what is despised by the people, and what is detrimental to their own interest, the king should not approve.

themes.justification: Section 10 explicitly addresses how the king should protect the internal rules of guilds and corporations while retaining authority to override rules contrary to royal interest or public welfare.

themes.topic: Impotency classifications and their legal consequences for marriage

mentions.quote: The wise have identified fourteen kinds of impotent men in the sacred texts. They are classified as curable and incurable.
The other four, beginning with the one impotent out of jealousy, should be abandoned like outcasts, even by a wife whose husband is alive.

themes.justification: The text devotes multiple consecutive verses to a fourteen-fold taxonomy of impotency, its curability, and the specific legal remedies available to wives in each case, making this a focused legal-medical sub-theme.

themes.topic: Pollution and moral hierarchy of mixed-caste (pratiloma vs. anuloma) offspring

mentions.quote: The most sinful in the mixed castes (`saṃkara`) is born with two classes in between in the reverse order (`prātilomyena`)
The birth that occurs in the regular order (`ānulomyena`) of the classes is remembered as the rule. The birth in the reverse order is remembered as the exception.

themes.justification: Although not explicitly labeled, the entire caste-mixture section is implicitly structured around a pollution gradient — the greater the class distance and the more hypogamous the union, the more sinful the offspring — an implicit moral logic underlying the taxonomy.

citations.quote: For violating an unwilling maiden, the punishment is the cutting off of two fingers. For violating a woman of a higher class, the middle amercement. (Nar. 12.71)
citations.justification: The verse reference '(Nar. 12.71)' embedded in the translated text is a self-citation marker indicating the text's own canonical verse numbering, attesting to an underlying Sanskrit source structure.

citations.quote: He who is a man with another woman but not a man with his own wife, she may take another husband. This is the ordinance of Nārada. (Nar. 12.19)
citations.justification: The explicit attribution 'This is the ordinance of Nārada' together with the verse number (Nar. 12.19) constitutes an internal self-citation establishing Nārada as the named authority for this specific ruling.
